cinema.name: Field Talkies
cinema.tagline: Short films that explain the hard parts of development practice. Pick one, or let them play in order.

films.title: The logframe: where it came from, what it breaks, when to use it
films.speaker: ImpactMojo
films.transcript: The logical framework was built in 1969 and 1970 for USAID, the United States aid agency. Leon Rosenberg led the work, first at Fry Consultants and then at his own firm, Practical Concepts Incorporated. The agency had a very specific problem. It could not tell which of its projects were working. And its objectives were written so vaguely that nobody could be held to them. The answer was a four by four matrix. Rows for goal, purpose, outputs and inputs. Columns for the narrative, the indicators, the means of verification, and the assumptions. Everything that annoys you about logframes, is already in that origin story. It was a contract management instrument, for a donor that could not supervise what it was funding. It was never a theory of how social change happens. In the 1980s, the German agency GTZ picked it up, and turned it into ZOPP. British aid made it close to mandatory. And by the 1990s, a procurement tool had become the standard way our sector was asked to think. First takeaway: logframes flatten causality. The matrix gives you one column of arrows, all going up. Inputs produce outputs, outputs produce purpose, and purpose contributes to goal. One direction, no loops, and no interaction between branches. There is no way to say that output two only works if output three has already landed, and the panchayat election has not just changed the block officer. Real programmes are full of feedback, and the format has no cell for feedback. Anything that does not fit gets pushed into the assumptions column, which is where the interesting content of most programmes goes to die. Des Gasper made this argument in the year 2000, in the journal Public Administration and Development. He wrote of logic-less frames, and of lock-frames: a matrix that gets frozen, and is then used for one-way accountability. Second takeaway, and this is the useful part: the logframe is a good communication tool. Hand someone a filled logframe, and in ninety seconds they know what the programme claims it will deliver, how it says it will know, and what needs to hold true. Try getting that from a twelve page theory of change with a spaghetti diagram. The failure is one of sequence. Teams open the template first, and think inside it. Instead, design the programme in whatever messy form the problem has. Argue about causality, draw the loops, and only then compress it into a logframe. Compression after thinking is fine. Compression as thinking is where the damage is. Third takeaway: know when it is the wrong format outright. The logframe works when the causal chain is short, well understood, and stable over the grant period. Examples are vaccination coverage, latrine construction and textbook distribution. It fails when the outcome depends on how other actors respond to you. It fails when the intervention has to change shape in year two. And it fails when the point is to shift a norm. Bakewell and Garbutt made this case for Sida in 2005. For that second category, use something built for emergence: outcome mapping, developmental evaluation, or process tracing. You will still have to produce a logframe for the donor, so produce it. Just do not confuse the document you filed with the thinking you did.
sources: Gasper, D. (2000). Evaluating the 'logical framework approach'. Public Administration and Development 20(1): 17-28.
Bakewell, O. and Garbutt, A. (2005). The Use and Abuse of the Logical Framework Approach. Sida.
Practical Concepts Incorporated (1979). The Logical Framework: A Manager's Guide.

films.title: Lead with the finding: presenting evidence to the people who decide
films.speaker: ImpactMojo
films.transcript: Here is a pattern you have seen. A presentation to a board, a state department, or a donor's programme team. Slide one, background. Slide two, methodology. Slide three, sampling frame and response rates. Slide seven, limitations. Slide eleven, findings. By slide four, three people are on their phones. And the one person who could act on your finding has decided this is a technical exercise rather than a decision aid. The sequence is backwards, and for a reason worth naming. We put method first because method is how we defend ourselves. It is where our credibility lives, and it feels like earning the right to be believed. Your audience reads it differently. They read it as: this person is not sure what they found. First point. Before you write anything, find out what decision the person in front of you is about to make, and when. A programme director deciding whether to renew a partner contract in six weeks needs something different from a board setting a three-year strategy. Same evaluation, same data, two completely different documents. If you do not know the decision, ask. It is a normal question, and people are usually relieved you asked it. If no decision is open, that is useful too. It tells you the finding will be filed, and that your energy belongs with whoever holds the next open decision. Second point. Lead with the finding. Sentence one is what you found. Sentence two is what it means for the decision. Method goes in the annex, where anyone who wants to check your work can find every bit of it. Nothing is hidden. The order follows what the reader needs first. Compare two versions of one result. Version one. We conducted a difference-in-differences analysis, using a matched comparison group of 412 households across 14 blocks, and found a statistically significant effect on savings behaviour at the 5 per cent level. Version two. Households in the programme are saving about 340 rupees more per month than comparable households outside it. That gap is large enough to matter for the credit component, and it is holding steady across all 14 blocks. It is the same study. The second version tells the reader what happened to real people, in units they use, and it points at the decision. Third point. Put your uncertainty in the same sentence as the finding. Keep it out of a limitations section at the end. About 340 rupees, and I would be surprised if the true figure were below 200 or above 500. That is honest, it is useful, and it takes four seconds. What people do instead is state the number with total confidence in the main text, and bury the caveats on slide nineteen, where nobody reads them. Then the number gets quoted back to them for years, stripped of every qualification. Non-technical audiences handle uncertainty all the time: in budgets, in politics, and in the weather. What they handle badly is uncertainty that arrives late, after they have already repeated your number in a meeting. So: their decision, your finding, your confidence. In that order. Method sits in the annex doing its job, which is being available to anyone who wants to check. The figures in this film are illustrative examples.

films.title: Welcome: what MEL really means
films.speaker: Varna
films.transcript: Hi folks, my name is Varna and a very warm welcome to all of you. Super happy to see you all here at ImpactMojo. Every year, organizations across South Asia spend crores collecting data on the programs they run: attendance sheets, beneficiary accounts, workshop photos. Most of it goes into a report, gets sent to a funder and sits there unread by December. That kind of data collection serves compliance. It really really serves decisions. MEL, as we all know, stands for monitoring, evaluation, and learning. Monitoring tracks whether a program is running as planned, are the supplements arriving, are the sessions happening, do the numbers match the work plan. Evaluation asks whether the program is achieving what it set out to achieve and for whom. Learning is what an organization does with those answers, feeding evaluation findings back into how the next field. ways gets designed. So the first takeaway, MEL exists to improve decisions. Take a nutrition program distributing supplements to children under 5. Monitoring tells you how many children received supplements this month, which matters to whoever manages the supply chain. What it doesn't do is it says nothing about whether nutritional status improved. Evaluation asks that question directly and it asks a harder one alongside it. Did nutritional status improve more for the children in this program than for children who were never reached by it at all. A program officer deciding whether to expand into three more blocks needs that second answer. The monitoring number on its own will not tell her whether expansion is worth the money. Second takeaway, MEL is not reporting, though the two get confused constantly. Reporting is retrospective. It documents what already happened, usually in a format under a specified condition and a specified way. Usually months after the events it describes. A mail system built properly runs alongside the program rather than actually trailing behind it. It gets designed from month 1, not assembled in month 11, because the annual report deadline is approaching. A program that waits until month 11 to build its mail system has already lost the chance to catch a failing activity back in month 3 while there was still time to fix it. By month Month 11, the year is spent and a report can only record what already went wrong. Third takeaway, good mail treats causality as a question to answer, not an assumption to make. Take literacy scores that rise in a district the same year an NGO runs a reading program there. Crediting the program is tempting, but scores could rise because the state issued new textbooks that year, because a good monsoon kept attendance steady through the term. or because of several other things moving in that district at the same time. So causal thinking asks what would have happened in the program's absence. Real comparison, a control group, a match district, a credible baseline measured before the program started. A rise in scores that happens near a program's timeline with no comparison behind it tells you very, very little. The same rise measured against a real counterfactual tells you what the program actually did. Mail exists to improve decisions. It is not the same activity as reporting and it treats causality as something to establish, not something to assume. We have a full course on this at impactmojo.in. Vandana should be able to share the link with you. It goes further into monitoring system design, evaluation methods and how to build learning loops that teams actually use rather than the ones that only get open during a donor review. I hope this video on what MEL is and why it matters, um, you know, serves as a useful, let's say 3-minute introduction and I look forward to a lot of our conversations going forward here. Thank you so much for joining.

films.title: What makes a good indicator?
films.speaker: ImpactMojo
films.transcript: Indicators, what makes a good one. An implementing partner reports that it distributed 40000 textbooks this year. The number is real, it is measurable and it goes straight into the quarterly report. What it does not tell you is whether a single child read a page further because of it. The gap between what gets counted and what actually matters is where most indicator design goes wrong. First takeaway, a good indicator measures what actually matters for the decision at hand, not what happens to be easy to count. Textbooks distributed is easy. Someone can count boxes at a warehouse. Reading comprehension improved is hard. It needs a test, administered consistently to a sample of children, compared against some kind of baseline. Programs gravitate towards the easy number because it is cheap and because it always moves in a reassuring direction. correction. Distribution figures only go up. The harder number is the one a decision maker actually needs before deciding whether to fund a second print run or redesign the whole approach. Second takeaway. Smart is necessary, but it's not sufficient. Every med training covers the smart criteria that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time bound. We all know this, right? They are worth knowing. going and an indicator that fails them is broken from the start. But smart only checks the shape of an indicator. It says nothing about whether the indicator is actually tracking the thing you care about. Number of training sessions held is specific. It's measurable, it's achievable, it's relevant to a training program and it's time bound to the reporting period. It is also almost useless for telling you whether the training changed anyone's behavior. Smart gets your well-formed indicator. It does not Get you a meaningful one. Third takeaway. Once an indicator becomes a target, people start optimizing for the indicator rather than the outcome it was meant to represent or what it was intended to achieve. This is sometimes called good hearts law after the economist who first stated it in the context of monetary policy. But the pattern shows up constantly in development work. Tell field staff that their performance is judged on the number of households in the country. visited and the household visits will rise. Sometimes by recording visits that lasted 90 seconds and covered well almost nothing. Tell teachers that attendance figures matter for a school's ranking and attendance registers can start looking really good, better than the classroom does. None of this requires bad faith. What happens is that when a proxy actually replaces the goal quietly and nobody actually notices the substitution because the number goes on the dashboard, they keep improving. But the three together and the practical test for any indicator is this. Does it track something a decision actually depends on? Does it hold up as a well-formed measure and can it survive becoming a target without collapsing into something that people can quietly gain. An indicator that passes the first two tests and fails the third will still mislead you just a little more slowly. The full The full course should be in a link that Vandana can share below. It covers an indicator design in more depth along with the sampling and baseline decisions that determine whether an indicator can even be interpreted once the data comes in or perhaps at a different time point. Happy reading. Please stay with us at Impact Motor.

films.title: Building a learning culture in your team
films.speaker: ImpactMojo
films.transcript: Hi everyone. today let's talk about building learning culture in our teams today where MEL fits in. So for a social impact organization a learning culture is the mechanism through which the organization gets better at solving problems than that that rarely have simple answers. what worked in one district may fail in another. A learning culture helps organizations notice, adapt, and improve rather than repeat the same assumptions. So what does learning culture mean for social impact organizations? In social sector, learning means asking, uh, what are we seeing on the ground? To what surprise does. Third, what is not working. Fourth, what are the communities? is teaching us. Fifth, how should we change our programs? So in learning culture exactly how our conversation changes. It changes with a. Staff can say I don't know without fear. Data is used for improvement, not only for reporting. Third, field insights travel across teams. Failures are examined, not hidden. And community is These are treated as source of knowledge rather than just beneficiaries. So teams can learn from program data, community, peers, and failed experiments. For this, there is a useful framework by Argus and Sean. It's called single loop versus double loop learning. So single loop learning says, where we ask a question, how can we do this activity? better. Example of the answer that it that can be for this question is improving attendance in a training program. In double loop learning, the question that we ask is, should we be doing this activity at all? And the answer to this question as an example could be, let's reconsider whether training is the right solution for the problem. So there can be three practical takeaways for leaders. To build a learning culture for your team using Mel. One is let's start creating psychological safety. You know, people learn faster when they can admit mistakes. Teams will not share real lessons if every discussion feels like an audit. So, some practical habits that we can build. One is we can end meetings with what did we learn this week? Or, you know, leaders can share their own mistakes first. Second takeaways, let's use data for learning, not just compliance. So many nonprofits collect data mainly for donors. We've been that. We've been there and done that. So, but high organize high learning organizations can ask, what does this data suggest? What should we change this next month? What questions remain unanswered? So research from the Urban Institute shows that learning cultures are strongly linked to continuous quality improvement. And third takeaway is build learning into routines. It has to be our daily habits and not just an occasional chance that we do in workshops. So let's create recurring structures where learning sits in our routine. It can be done in following ways. One is monthly reflection meetings. Second, after action reviews. Third, peer feedback sessions. Fourth, feed learning notes. And fifth is quarterly learning briefs. And remember, all this has to be done in a environment that promotes psychological safety, that allows to share mistakes and pitfalls. Because research shows that again, the learning culture becomes effective when learning Learning is embedded in the way work is done. To end, I would say the way we need to reframe social impact, um, requires perhaps a shift in the way we think, where we say that monitoring us whether activities happened, evaluation us whether change happened, but a learning culture asks what should happen. Next. That is where evidence becomes action and where organizations become more effective over time.

films.title: Baseline design: the decisions that matter
films.speaker: ImpactMojo
films.transcript: Hello, today we're talking about baseline design and the decisions that matter. A baseline is often treated as a formality to go out before the program starts, collect some numbers, file them away, move on to implementation. Done that way, unfortunately, a baseline is close to worthless. The decisions made at baseline stage determine whether anything collected afterward can actually be interpreted, and most of those decisions get made in the first two weeks of a project under time pressure by whoever happens to be available. at that particular point in time. So the first takeaway, a baseline without a counterfactual is just a photograph or at least close enough. A photograph tells you what conditions look like at one point in time. It does not tell you what would have happened without the program. If literacy rates in a district were 40% before an intervention and 50% two years later, that 10 point rise means very little on its own. Rates could have risen anyway from a new textbook policy from a good run of school attendance, you know, from a state government scheme, maybe a growth effect of the child itself running in parallel. A baseline earns the name only when it is paired with a comparison group, a control, a math set of villages or schools that did not receive the program, so that the 10 point rise can be checked against what happened in places the program never touched or where it never happened at all. Without that comparison, a baseline records a starting point and enough nothing more. Kind of like knowing where a day starts but not much else. Second takeaway, sampling choices made at baseline constraint everything downstream and they are close to impossible to fix later. If the baseline sample skews towards villages near a main road for example because they were easier to reach, every end line comparison inherits that skew. If a matched comparison group was selected using criteria that turn out to differ from the treatment group in some Some way that matters no amount of statistical adjustment fully repairs at that end line. Sample size decided at baseline sets the limit on what effect sizes the evaluation will ever be able to detect with any confidence and that limit does not move no matter how good the end line fieldwork is. These are not decisions to delegate to whoever is free at that point in time in that week. They need someone who understands what the evaluation is meant to detect, deciding beforehand. before a single household is visited because a sampling frame that is built on wrong logic cannot be corrected after the fact. It can only be lived with and that pain will never go away. Third takeaway, document your methodology, not your numbers. 2 years after a baseline, someone will ask how the comparison group was selected, what the exact wording of a key question was, whether a particular village was excluded. and why. If the answer lives only in the memory of whoever ran the field work, and that person has since left, moved on, or gone to a different organization, the baseline becomes unusable at exactly the moment it was supposed to be off, which is at the end line when it needs to be compared with something. A spreadsheet of baseline numbers without a methodology note or context attached to a set of figures, nobody can defend under scrutiny. The note should record the sample. sampling frame, the selection criteria for any comparison group, the exact survey instrument used, and any deviations from the original design because there are always some deviations. That documentation is what turns a baseline from a fixed artifact into evidence that can withstand quite a serious question 2 years later. Taking together these three decisions, the counterfactual, the sampling design, and the documentation. are what separate a baseline that supports a real evaluation from one that produces a number that nobody can trust once anyone asks how was it built. We have a course which is again you know on sampling in particular and evaluation design. Vandana should be able to share the link of the series and the rest of the advanced track with you. Stay with ImpactMojo. Happy learning.

films.title: Learning in MEL: learning, not reporting
films.speaker: Varna
films.transcript: In most MEL frameworks I have read, the L sits at the end of the acronym and at the end of the budget. It gets a line. Learnings will be documented and shared with stakeholders. Nobody argues with that sentence. Have you thought why? It's actually exactly the problem with it. So let me give you a working definition. Learning happened if someone with the authority to change something changed it because of evidence. And that evidence that your system produced, that's the whole test. Not documentation, not dissemination, a change decision. So try it on your own project, right? Name one decision in the last 12 months or 15 months. that actually went differently because of your M&E data. If you can name it, say what the decision was, who made it, and which number of findings specifically move them. If you cannot name one, your system is producing accountability, which I think is a legitimate function, but it's not the same thing as learning. Now the second point, and this is where I think most of us get stuck, right? Learning is not the same as completing an evaluation, checking a box, right? An evaluation is an event. It has a TOR, an inception report, a field phase, a draft, maybe a validation workshop, a final report. Everyone involved is heavily incentivized to kind of finish it, complete it, report it, done. Almost nobody incentivized for what happens after it. The report lands in April, the program design was locked in in the previous November. The next design window, it opens in 18 months from now. So the evaluation can be technically excellent and still arrive at a moment when no decision is open. The finding has actually, how do I say this plainly? It has nowhere to go. So this is Patton's old argument in utilization focused evaluation. And it has been sitting there since 1978 without being taken seriously enough. What Patton asks you is to identify the specific people who will use the findings and the specific decisions they face before you design anything at all. Named people. real decisions with real dates, which brings me to the third point. Learning is a scheduled activity, otherwise it's fiction. So think about how ruthlessly we schedule everything else, right, in our lives. Or even in M&E, baseline in month three, midline in month 18, quarterly reports on the 15th, all of it is in the work plan. And all All of it is costly, all of it with somebody's name on it. Then learning kind of goes or gets into ongoing reflection and no budget line. Put it in the calendar instead, a quarterly session, 90 minutes with two or three people who can actually authorize a change to how the program is being rolled out. Bring three findings, not 30, not 50. For each one, the question on the table is, does this change what we do next quarter? Yes or no? If the answer is no, say so loudly, and you also need to record why. That's a legitimate outcome. We looked and we are staying the course, and here is our reason. This is a learning record. Silence on why a decision took place or didn't is not. One more thing. worth saying because it is uncomfortable. A lot of what gets called learning in our sector is retrospective justification. The program design was set by a donor's theory of change or by what the last grant funded or by what the team already knows how to do. The M&E data arrives afterwards and then it gets read for evidence that the choice was made. actually found, but was it? Everyone recognizes this when it happens elsewhere. And nobody actually recognizes it in their own project or their own program that they're taking ownership for. The defense against it is boring and it's procedural. Write it down before the data comes in. What results would make you kind of change course. Then check whether that result actually arrived, did it actually happen on the ground. This is learning. Everything else, in my view, is reporting.

films.title: Designing gender-sensitive FGDs and KIIs
films.speaker: Vandana
films.transcript:
Hi everyone. Welcome to PLC Group. Today, in this microlearning video, we will talk about designing gender-sensitive focus group discussions and key informant interviews. When we say gender-sensitive research, we often think about one thing first: do we include both women and men in our sample? But gender-sensitive qualitative research is much more than that. Because in an FGD or KII, who is in the room, who is asking the question, and how the conversation is structured can all shape the evidence we get. So here are three things to think about when designing gender-sensitive FGDs and KIIs.

Takeaway one: who you include determines what you can learn. Before designing your FGD or KII, don't just ask, "Who is your target population?" Ask, "Whose experience do we need to understand?" For example, if you're studying girls' access to secondary education, talking only to girls may tell you about their experience. But talking separately to girls, boys, parents, teachers and school leaders may reveal something different about gender norms and power relationships shaping those experiences. And importantly, don't assume that women or men are homogeneous groups. Age, caste, class, disability, marital status, geography, sexuality, occupation and other social identities can intersect with gender. So your sampling should reflect the differences that matter for your research question. UN Women specifically emphasises that gender-sensitive data collection needs to reflect the realities of different groups, and that qualitative methods such as KIIs and FGDs can be used to surface these differences.

Takeaway two: who is in the room changes what is said. This is particularly important for FGDs. Imagine asking adolescent girls about mobility restrictions in a group that includes their father, male teachers, or community leaders. Will they speak in exactly the same way? Probably not. Because power relations, social expectation, and concerns about judgment can influence what people are willing to disclose. That is why group composition matters. You may need separate groups based on gender, age, social position and other characteristics, particularly when discussing sensitive issues. And don't forget the facilitator. The gender, age, social position and perceived authority of the interviewer can also influence the interaction. There is research from Bihar, for example, that explored how interviewers' gender affected women's responses to questions about household and maternal health, highlighting that interviewer characteristics can matter in traditional settings. So don't treat the facilitator as invisible. The researcher is part of the research environment.

Takeaway three: how you ask determines what becomes visible. A gender-sensitive interview guide is not simply "What problems do women face?" That question already assumes women have problems and may completely miss the underlying system. Instead, can we ask questions that explore roles, expectations, decision-making and power? For example, instead of "Do women participate in household financial decisions?", let's try "Who usually makes decisions about how household money is spent? Can you give an example of a recent decision?" Then you can probe further and ask: who was consulted? Who had the final say? Would this be different for a man, a woman or a third-gender person in the same situation? These questions move us from individual characteristics to relationships, norms and structure, and that's often where gender becomes visible.

And finally, remember that FGDs and KIIs serve different purposes. FGDs are particularly useful for understanding shared norms, language, expectation, and differences within a group. KIIs can help us understand institutions, systems, decision-making, and the perspective of people with particular knowledge or role. So before your next FGD or KII, pause and ask three questions. Who needs to be in the room? Who might speak differently because of who else is in the room? And what questions will help us uncover gendered roles, norms and power, rather than simply document differences between women, men and third gender? Because gender-sensitive qualitative research isn't just about collecting data from women and men. It is about designing the research so that gendered experiences and power relationships have a chance to become visible. Thank you, and have a great week.

films.title: What gender-sensitive MEL actually asks
films.speaker: Vandana
films.transcript:
Hi everyone, hope you are reading and enjoying and learning from the PLC group. Today let's talk about what gender-sensitive MEL is. When we say gender-sensitive MEL, many of us immediately think we need to disaggregate our data by sex. So we count how many women participated, how many men participated. And yes, that is important. But gender-sensitive MEL goes beyond counting. Because knowing that sixty percent of participants were women doesn't tell us whether women actually had equal access, benefited equally, or experienced the programme in the same way.

Let's take a simple example. Imagine a hundred people attend a skill training programme. Sixty are women. Great. We might say women's participation is strong. But then we ask: did women attend regularly? Did they have time to participate alongside unpaid care and household responsibilities? Did they have access to transport or digital devices? After training, were they able to use those skills? And if they earned an income, did they have control over that income? Now we are asking gender-sensitive MEL questions.

Gender-sensitive MEL recognises that gender is not just a category in our data. Gender shapes people's roles, access to resources, decision-making, time, mobility and power. So instead of asking only how many men or women participated, we also ask: did women and men experience the programme differently? If so, why? And did the programme change anything about these differences?

This also changes what we measure. For example, instead of only measuring how many women received financial support, we might also ask how many women have independent access to and control over that support. Instead of just counting women in a community meeting, we ask: were women able to speak? Were their views included in the decisions? So we move from measuring participation to understanding access, benefit, voice, control and power.

And finally, gender-sensitive MEL is not just about collecting better data. It is about using what we learn to adapt our programmes. If we find that women are dropping out because sessions clash with their care responsibilities, what do we change? If women participate but don't control the benefits, what do we need to redesign? That's when MEL becomes a tool for gender equality, not just for reporting.

So here's a key takeaway. Sex-disaggregated data tells us who participated. Gender-sensitive MEL asks how gender shaped their experiences, outcomes and power, and what we need to do differently because of what we find. And here, when we say gender, we mean men, women and other third-gender categories. For this week's PLC discussion, I would welcome all of us to take one indicator from your own programme and ask: what am I missing if I only disaggregate this data by gender? Thank you, and have a great weekend.

films.title: Why causal inference: improvement is not impact
films.speaker: Vandana
films.transcript: Everyone, good morning and welcome to a new month focusing on a new topic which is on causal inference for practitioners. So today in this micro learning video we are going to talk specifically about what is causal inference and why do practitioners like us need it. So let's say you run a program, maybe it could be a scholarship program, a teacher training program, livelihood or a digital learning program. Six months later, you see the data and you see improvement. So you say our program worked. But did it really work? That simple question is where causal inference begins. So what is causal inference? Causal inference is about answering a very specific question. That is, what changed because of our intervention? Not simply did things improve, But did they improve because of what we did? Imagine a program that provides smartphone and digital learning content to children in rural India. After a year, their test scores go up, which is great. But what would their scores have been if they had not received our program? That is the counterfactual. And we can never observe both outcomes for the same child at the same time, the outcome with the program and the outcome without it. That is the fundamental problem of causal inference. So, the first takeaway is improvement is not same as impact. Suppose children in remedial education program improve their reading scores from 40 to 55 and it is tempting to say that oh our program improved learning by 15 points. But perhaps the school year itself would have produced 10 points of improvement before the intervention. Or perhaps the children who joined the program were already more motivated or perhaps Another government initiative reached the same school at the same time. So the real question is not did the numbers go up. It is how much of the change can we credibly attribute to our program. Now takeaway two, correlation doesn't simply mean causation. This sounds like a statistic textbook statement but it matters enormously in our everyday program work. So imagine we find that districts with higher participation in a women's livelihood programme also have higher household incomes. But does it mean that the program increased incomes? Not necessarily. Perhaps the program was implemented more strongly in districts that were already economically better off. Perhaps women who were more economically active were more likely to participate. Or another factor is driving both the participation and income. So this is This is a selection bias. What are the first problems that practitioners need to recognize when making causal claims? Now takeaway three. Causal inference is not one method, it is a way of thinking. An RCT may help when you can randomly assign treatment, but that's not always possible or ethical in development programs. So we have other designs. One, matching. It can help create more comparable groups. Two, difference in differences can compare changes over time when its assumptions are credible. Regression discontinuity can be useful when programme eligibility is determined by clear cut off. Instrumental variables and synthetic controls can answer other kinds of causal questions. And causal machine learning can help us explore who benefits and how effects vary. So the important point is you don't choose a method because it sounds sophisticated, you choose it because it gives you a credible way to construct missing counterfactual. That is why our course for this month, with reference to which our discussion will be held, is based on identification before estimation. The assumptions come before the regression. And you don't have to be an econometrician to need causal inference. If you design programs, it helps you ask better evaluation questions, if you commission evaluation, it helps you judge whether proposed design can actually answer your question. If you read evaluation reports, it helps you distinguish a strong causal claim from a weak association. And if you work in MEL, it helps you move beyond we reach 10,000 people towards a much harder question. What changed because we reached them? Thank you and hope you find this video useful.

films.title: What rigorous measurement looks like: the WEAI
films.speaker: Vandana
films.transcript: Hi everyone, welcome to yet another micro learning video for this week. The theme that we are covering is gender M&E. Today we will talk about the Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index. What does rigorous measurement actually look like? When we say we need rigorous measurement, what do we really mean? Does it mean more indicators, a long questionnaire, a sophisticated system? distinguished model, not necessarily. A useful example is Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index, WEAI, which is developed by IFPRI, OPHI and the Feed the Future initiative. This index was created because something as important as women's empowerment is actually quite difficult to measure. Think about a program that says we have empowered women farmers. How would you measure that? You could count how many women attended training, how many women received agricultural inputs, how many women started earning income. All of these are useful indicators, but none of them on their own tell us whether a woman actually has greater agency or decision-making power. And that is where WEAI becomes interesting. So this index actually looks at empowerment across 5 domains. One, production. Who operates in and makes decisions about agriculture production? Second, resources. Who has access to and control over land, livestock, credit, and other resources? Third, income. Who decides how income is used? And fourth, leadership. Can women participate and have a voice in community programs? And last, time. How is the time divided between productive work, domestic work and leisure. It also looks at gender parity, essentially asking how women's empowerment compares with what men in the same households experience. Now what makes this as a useful example of rigorous measurement? First, it defines the concept before measuring it. Empowerment is not left as a vague idea. The researchers break it down into dimensions that can actually be investigated. Second, it doesn't rely on single proxy. Having an income doesn't automatically mean having control over that income. Owning an asset doesn't necessarily mean being able to decide how it is used. And participating in a meeting doesn't necessarily mean having influence in that meeting. So the measure tries to distinguish between these things. And third, the methodology is explicit. This index uses defined indicators, thresholds, and an aggregation methodology. That means we can examine how the measures were constructed rather than simply accepting a number because it comes from a survey. And fourth, and this is perhaps the most important lesson, the measure itself has been tested and refined. The original index was piloted in different countries and later versions such as pro-WEAI were developed and tested for agricultural development programs. Pictures have also examined how individual questions and indicators perform across different context. So rigorous here doesn't mean we created a complicated index. therefore it must be rigorous. It means measurement has been conceptually grounded, operationalized, tested, examined and revised. Hope you liked this video and you find this useful. Thank you.

films.title: Feminist evaluation: whose knowledge counts
films.speaker: Vandana
films.transcript: Hi everyone, welcome to the micro learning video two of this week. Today we will spend some time talking about feminist evaluation and what it actually means. When we hear feminist evaluation, we may immediately think of evaluations about women, gender, indicators, or perhaps collecting data separately for women and men and third gender. But feminist evaluation is asking a much more fundamental question. What happens when we bring feminist theory into the way we understand evaluation itself? At its core, feminist evaluation challenges the idea that evaluation is a completely neutral process of producing objective knowledge because before we collect any data, we have already made choices. What is worth measuring? What counts as evidence? Whose experience is credible? Who gets to define the evaluation questions? and who ultimately gets to use the knowledge that an evaluation produces. These are not only methodological questions, they are questions about power and knowledge. One of the fundamental texts in feminist evaluation by Sielbeck-Bowen and colleagues identifies multiple ways of knowing as a central principle. It argues that knowledge is socially, culturally, and historically situated and that some forms of knowledge are systematically privileged over others. So for example, imagine an evaluation where a program reports that women's economic empowerment has improved because household income has increased. A feminist evaluator might reject that indicator, but she might ask whose definition of empowerment are we using? Does increased income necessarily mean greater decision-making power? Who controls that income? Has unpaid care work changed? Has mobility changed? Has the woman's ability to negotiate decisions within the household changed? The point is not that one kind of data is automatically better than the other. The point is that the way we frame the questions determines what becomes visible as knowledge. And this brings us to another important theoretical distinction. First, participatory does not automatically mean feminist. I think we've spoken about this earlier in the video. Participation tells us something about who is involved. A feminist lens asks us to examine how power operates within that participation. Who sets the agenda, who speaks, who remains silent, whose knowledge is treated as authoritative, and who has the power to interpret what participants have said. So a focus group with women can be participatory without necessarily challenging the underlying power relations of the evaluation. That is why feminist evaluation is better understood as a theoretical orientation rather than a particular method. You can use a survey, interviews, administrative data, participatory method. The method itself does not make an evaluation feminist. The feminist lens changes the question we bring to the method. And in the South Asian context, this becomes even more important. Gender doesn't operate in isolation, caste, class, religion, sexuality, disability, age and geography can shape whose experiences are visible, whose knowledge is valued. Radhika Govinda's work on gender evaluation in South Asia specifically examines this theoretical terrain and questions how conventional evaluation approaches understand changes in gender relations in contexts such as India. So perhaps three theoretical questions can help us recognize a feminist evaluation. First, whose knowledge is being produced and whose knowledge is being privileged. Second, what power relations shape the production and interpretation of that knowledge? And third, what assumptions about gender, inequality, and social change are built into evaluation itself? Hope you find this video useful. Thank you.

films.title: Community score cards as an MEL practice
films.speaker: Vandana
films.transcript: Hi everyone, welcome to this week's first micro learning video. We will be talking about using community scorecards as an MEL practice. When we hear community scorecard, we often imagine a simple exercise. Ask the community to rate a service from 1 to 5. But a well designed community scorecard can be much more useful than that. It can become an MEL process for understanding experience, generating evidence and creating a conversation between communities and program teams. So, how can we actually use it? First, start with what you want to learn, not with the scorecard. For example, suppose you are running a maternal health program. Instead of asking how satisfied are you with the healthcare service or healthcare center, you could ask, can women actually access the service they are entitled to? That immediately opens different questions like, can they reach the center? Are the timings workable? Do they need someone's permission to travel? Do they feel comfortable speaking to the health worker? And importantly, do different groups experience the service differently? That is what a gender lens can become part of your MEL design. Second, don't assume that one community conversation represents the whole community. A community scorecard process can create different spaces for different groups to discuss their experiences. For example, women may discuss health service separately from men. Adolescent girls may have a different set of concerns. People with disabilities may identify barriers that others simply don't notice. So the point isn't to create endless groups, the point is just to ask whose experience might disappear if we put everyone in the same room. Third, don't stop at the scorecard alone. That is probably the most important one. Imagine women give a health center a score 2 out of 5. Now the number itself isn't very useful. The real MEL evidence is in the conversation that follows, like why they give 2. What happened? Who is affected? Is this one-off problem or something people experience repeatedly? What would a 4 look like? And what can the community and service provider actually change. Now your scorecard has generated qualitative evidence, quantitative evidence, and an action agenda. And finally, close the loop. A scorecard becomes much more meaningful when the next round asks what's changed after we raise these issues. It may be the center has changed timings, maybe women reported feeling safer, or whatever it may be. And that is also a valuable MEL evidence. So if you're thinking about using a community scorecard in your program, don't begin with what question should be put in the scorecard, begin with these three questions: whose experience do we need to understand? What would meaningful change look like to them? And what will we do with what we learn? Because strength of community scorecard isn't really the score, it's the process of turning community experience into evidence. and evidence into action. In this case, CARE's Community Score Card process is particularly useful because communities don't simply give a score. They identify issues, develop indicators, and explain why they have a particular score and discuss possible improvements with the service providers. Hope you find this video useful. Thank you
